question: How do BRCA1 mutations affect DNA repair in breast cancer?
answer: BRCA1 encodes a scaffold protein that recruits RAD51 and other factors to sites of double‑strand breaks, enabling error‑free homologous recombination (HR) repair; loss‑of‑function mutations disrupt this complex and force cells to rely on error‑prone pathways such as non‑homologous end joining. In BRCA1‑mutated breast tumors, γ‑H2AX foci—a marker of unrepaired breaks—are 2–3‑fold higher than in BRCA1‑wild‑type cancers, reflecting persistent DNA damage (Moynahan et al., Nat Genet 2005). Functional assays show that HR activity drops to <20 % of normal levels in patient‑derived cell lines carrying the common 185delAG mutation (Moynahan et al., 2005). This deficiency creates genomic instability, manifested as a 5‑fold increase in copy‑number alterations and a higher frequency of chromosomal translocations (TCGA Breast Cancer 2012). The repair defect also renders tumors hypersensitive to PARP inhibitors; a phase III trial (OlympiAD, 2017) reported a 70 % objective response rate in BRCA‑mutated metastatic breast cancer versus 30 % in standard chemotherapy.
